Canada operates one of the most generous and technically rigorous R&D tax incentive regimes in the industrialized world, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) and the Income Tax Regulations. Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential legislative overhaul since 2012. Enacted via Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal government doubled the enhanced 35% SR&ED expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, expanded the corporate phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and shared-use-equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024. Simultaneously, at the provincial level, Quebec enacted a sweeping structural reform for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, abolishing eight legacy R&D tax credits and replacing them with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (including capital equipment) above an exclusion threshold, and 20% on excess expenditures.
1. Executive Summary and the 2025–2026 Legislative Transformation
1.1 Overview of Canada's Dual-Pillar Innovation Tax Architecture

The Canadian federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Program is jointly administered by two federal bodies with distinct statutory mandates. The Department of Finance Canada establishes the legislative framework and tax policy encoded in Section 37, Section 127, Section 127.1, and Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, alongside Sections 2900 to 2903 (and Part XI for Capital Cost Allowance) of the Income Tax Regulations. Operational administration, technical eligibility evaluation, financial audit verification, and tax processing are executed by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).
The federal SR&ED programme delivers financial support to businesses carrying on R&D in Canada through two distinct, sequential statutory mechanisms:

items: Immediate Income Tax Deduction and Indefinite Pool Carryforward (Section 37): Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, eligible capital SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)). The resulting pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures may be deducted in full or in part to reduce net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year.

SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (Section 127 and Section 127.1): Under subsection 127(5) and subsection 127(9), a taxpayer earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Earned ITCs first offset federal Part I income tax otherwise payable; any unused ITCs may either be refunded in cash under section 127.1 (up to 100% for current expenditures and 40% for capital expenditures of eligible Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations [ECPCs] within their expenditure limit) or carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years under subsection 127(9).

body.text: Layered atop the federal SR&ED regime is a comprehensive network of provincial and territorial R&D tax incentives across nine provinces and one territory. With the exception of Quebec (where corporate tax credits are administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (where the Innovation Employment Grant [IEG] is administered by the province under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act), provincial and territorial R&D tax credits in Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon are administered directly by the CRA on behalf of the respective governments through the federal T2 corporate or T1 individual income tax system.
1.2 Enactment of Bill C-15 (March 26, 2026) and the Post-December 15, 2024 Federal Regime

For over a decade following the 2012 federal budget reforms (which took effect in 2013 and 2014), the SR&ED programme operated under restricted parameters: capital expenditures and equipment lease payments were eliminated after December 31, 2013; the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) overhead rate was reduced from 65% (2012 and prior) to 60% (2013) and 55% (2014 onward); arm's-length contract payments and third-party payments were restricted to 80% inclusion for ITC purposes; the basic ITC rate was reduced from 20% to 15%; and the enhanced 35% ITC remained capped at a $3,000,000 expenditure limit restricted to CCPCs.

Following legislative proposals introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) and Budget 2025, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Any tax guidance, financial models, or compliance software relying on pre-2025 parameters is outdated and will misstate corporate entitlements.

Under the enacted Bill C-15 legislation, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC (subsection 127(10.1)) is doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. Consequently, the maximum annual cash refund on current SR&ED expenditures for an eligible corporation increases from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Simultaneously, for CCPCs with taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada threshold at which the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to phase out increases from $10,000,000 to $15,000,000, and the upper threshold at which the expenditure limit is completely eliminated increases from $50,000,000 to $75,000,000.

Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(10.1) and subsection 127(10.6) extend the enhanced 35% refundable ITC up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). (While the 2024 Fall Economic Statement had proposed a $4.5 million limit, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 enacted the $6,000,000 limit for both CCPCs and ECPCs). An ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out when its average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (as reported on financial statements or consolidated financial statements) is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Under new subsection 127(10.32), a CCPC or an associated group of CCPCs may also elect to calculate its expenditure limit using this three-year average annual revenue method rather than prior-year taxable capital.

Effective for depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), and for equipment lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024, capital expenditures are restored to both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (paragraph 37(1)(b)) and Section 127 qualified expenditures. Capital expenditures meeting the "all or substantially all" (ASA — 90% or more) test qualify at 100%, while new equipment used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) for SR&ED qualifies under the restored Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) regime at 25% of capital cost in each of two consecutive periods (50% total). Enhanced 35% ITCs earned on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit are 40% refundable in cash. Consequentially, former subsection 37(14) (the capital "look-through rule" that reduced subcontractor and third-party claims by the performer's capital costs) is repealed for expenditures after December 15, 2024. Finally, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process accessible via My Business Account, allowing claimants to submit proposed R&D project plans prior to starting work or incurring expenditures and receive a formal technical eligibility determination from the CRA within 8 weeks.

body.text: 1.3 Provincial Restructuring: Quebec's Consolidation into the CRIC Regime

Parallel to the federal modernization, the Government of Quebec enacted a major overhaul of its provincial R&D tax system in the 2025–2026 Quebec Budget (detailed in Quebec Finance Bulletin 2025-6). For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec repealed eight separate R&D tax credits—most notably the legacy R&D Salaries and Wages Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.7, which previously provided a base rate of 14% for many claimants). In their place, Quebec established the single, consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation, designated by Revenu Québec as the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization and claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T).
The CRIC alters R&D tax planning in Quebec across four dimensions:

items: Higher Base Refundable Rates for All Corporations: The CRIC is 100% refundable and provides 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the exclusion threshold and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000, with no corporate asset-size test or CCPC restriction. Large enterprises and foreign-owned subsidiaries operating in Quebec access the same 30% first-tier and 20% second-tier refundable rates as small CCPCs.

Coverage of Pre-Commercialization Activities: Beyond pure SR&ED (which remains harmonized with the federal definition under subsection 248(1) and subject to CRA scientific review), the CRIC extends tax credit eligibility to pre-commercialization activities conducted in Quebec in conjunction with R&D performed in Quebec—specifically regulatory compliance testing, technological validations for initial certification, and product design (form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and material selection).

Inclusion of Capital Property Acquisitions: Aligning with the federal restoration of capital costs, the CRIC includes 100% of property acquisition costs (depreciable capital equipment used in Quebec for R&D or pre-commercialization, excluding land and buildings or rights to use them) as qualified expenditures.

Unified Exclusion Threshold: A claimant's total qualified CRIC expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the applicable Basic Personal Amount (BPA) of the personal income tax system (reported by tax advisory guides as $18,571 for 2025 and $18,952 for 2026) for each eligible employee, prorated by the time spent by that employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.

body.text: 2. Statutory Framework and Eligibility Criteria Under the Federal Income Tax Act
2.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED in Subsection 248(1)

The legal gateway to all federal SR&ED deductions and Investment Tax Credits—as well as provincial and territorial R&D tax credits across Canada—is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act. This definition was not altered by Bill C-15.

Under subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of three core categories (paragraphs (a), (b), or (c)):

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research is typically conducted in laboratory environments to understand fundamental phenomena, with results often published in scientific journals (for example, studying a newly discovered virus to better understand its characteristics).

Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Applied research seeks to generate new scientific knowledge directed toward a practical objective (for example, efforts to develop a vaccine against a new virus by exploiting identified characteristics of that newly discovered virus).

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development is the most commonly claimed category of SR&ED in Canada. Notably, the statutory phrase "including incremental improvements thereto" confirms that an eligible project does not need to create a brand-new product category; iterative, incremental technological advancements in existing products or manufacturing processes qualify, provided they seek to advance underlying technological knowledge or capability rather than applying standard practice.

body.text: 2.2 Eligible Support Work Under Paragraph 248(1)(d) Versus Excluded Activities Under Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Once a claimant establishes that core work under paragraph 248(1)(a), (b), or (c) has been undertaken in Canada, paragraph 248(1)(d) expands the scope of eligible SR&ED to include support work. Specifically, paragraph (d) encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight statutory categories:

items: Engineering;
Design (defined in the CRA glossary as work to transform concepts and ideas into a plan);
Operations research;
Mathematical analysis;
Computer programming;
Data collection;
Testing; and
Psychological research.

body.text: For any activity within these eight categories to qualify as SR&ED under paragraph 248(1)(d), it must satisfy two cumulative statutory conditions: the work must be commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of core basic research, applied research, or experimental development work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work is not SR&ED on its own. In an April 24, 2015 glossary revision, the CRA removed the term "routine engineering" to clarify that there is no statutory differentiation between engineering and routine engineering; while engineering practice on its own is not eligible, engineers frequently perform basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible support work.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the Income Tax Act establish seven categories of excluded work that cannot be claimed as SR&ED. These statutory exclusions cover: (e) market research or sales promotion (work that supplements advertising and personal selling, coordinating them and making them effective); (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities (Note: management is considered a social science and is excluded under paragraph (g), whereas psychological research that is directly in support of and commensurate with the needs of basic research, applied research, or experimental development is eligible under paragraph (d)); (h) prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas (Note: if a business conducts SR&ED while prospecting for minerals, it may claim the eligible SR&ED work while excluding the mineral prospecting work, subject to specific exclusions in subsection 127(9) for trenching, digging test pits, and preliminary sampling other than specified sampling); (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection.

As emphasized in the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, the decisive feature distinguishing support work under paragraph (d) from excluded work under paragraphs (e) to (k) is purpose—that is, why the work was done. If data collection is carried out as a routine activity to support normal business operations (such as quality assurance or quality control), it is excluded. If data collection is carried out specifically to directly support scientific research or experimental development work, it qualifies as eligible support work. Similarly, under the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, when experimental development is performed during a production run, the context may be experimental development with experimental production (ED+EP) or experimental development with commercial production (ED+CP). Only the production output required to evaluate the technical aspects of the SR&ED project constitutes experimental production; any production beyond what is required for the SR&ED is classified as "excess production", and all labour, overhead, and material costs relating to excess production or commercial production (CP) are disallowed.
2.3 The CRA's "Why" and "How" Eligibility Requirements Versus the Five Questions
Understanding the evolution of the CRA's administrative eligibility framework is critical for both preparing Form T661 narratives and defending claims during audit or litigation.

From 2012 until summer 2021, the CRA evaluated technical eligibility using five sequential questions set out in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012, revised in 2015, and archived in 2021), which directly reflected the five-part judicial approach established by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC). In summer 2021 (with subsequent updates in July 2022 and August 2025), the CRA replaced the archived five-questions policy with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, presenting two requirements—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement—derived from the unchanged statutory definition in subsection 248(1).

Canada, 2022 FCA 72, the CRA's 2021 eligibility guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method established in Northwest Hydraulic. Both the "Why" and the "How" requirements must be met simultaneously: systematic work aimed at a routine goal fails the "Why" requirement, while a genuine technological goal pursued by trial and error with no hypothesis or records fails the "How" requirement.
2.4 Establishing the Knowledge Baseline, Technological Uncertainty, and Conceptual Advancement

In CRA technical reviews, the central analytical inquiry is whether the claimant faced genuine scientific or technological uncertainty and sought scientific or technological advancement. The CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives establish four governing principles applied by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) during technical reviews.

First, scientific or technological uncertainty arises only when it is unknown or uncertain whether a given result or objective can be achieved due to an insufficiency in available scientific or technological knowledge. Available knowledge is defined as the combined scientific or technological knowledge of the resources within the claimant's business together with public sources reasonably available to the business. Acquiring existing available knowledge or know-how through staff training, hiring external experts or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not meet the technological advancement requirement. Similarly, circumventing a technological uncertainty through a workaround that relies on available knowledge renders the work ineligible.

Second, in experimental development projects (such as scaling up and optimizing a production process), an insufficiency in available technological knowledge is typically characterized by situations where existing design methods are non-applicable, specifications do not conform to established standards, too many variables or unknowns exist, operating conditions fall outside the normal range, the nature of the problem is evolving, required data is not readily available, or interlocking constraints exist. While reasonable cost targets on their own do not create technological uncertainty, attempting to meet economic constraints can create an underlying technological uncertainty that qualifies for SR&ED.

Third, to satisfy the "Why" requirement, the work must seek the generation or discovery of conceptual knowledge (such as theories or prediction models) that advances the understanding of science or technology, rather than merely collecting factual knowledge (such as empirical data or measurements).

Fourth, success or failure in meeting the technical objectives is not relevant when assessing whether work meets the "Why" requirement. The statutory definition in subsection 248(1) requires only that the purpose of the work be to achieve scientific or technological advancement.
3. Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and Corporate Tax Mechanics
3.1 Structure and Indefinite Carryforward of the Subsection 37(1) Expenditure Pool

The first financial incentive under the federal SR&ED programme is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures governed by subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act and calculated in Section C of Part 3 of Form T661.

Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year may pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and—for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024—eligible capital SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the taxpayer. While Form T661 calculates the current-year amount available for deduction by adjusting the prior-year ending pool balance, the legislation is structured as a cumulative running pool that accumulates amounts over time and is recalculated taking into account all relevant transactions and adjustments over that period.

Deduction from the subsection 37(1) pool is optional in any taxation year. A claimant may deduct the entire available pool balance, any partial amount up to the available balance at the end of the taxation year (claimed on Form T2SCH1), or nothing at all, carrying the positive balance forward. A positive balance in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures does not expire; it can be carried forward indefinitely and deducted in any subsequent taxation year against business income. Furthermore, deducting an amount from an existing Section 37 pool balance in a subsequent year is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, provided the underlying SR&ED expenditures were properly identified on Form T661 on time for the year in which they were incurred.
3.2 Statutory Additions, Deductions, and Negative Pool Balance Recapture Under Paragraph 12(1)(v)
The subsection 37(1) pool balance is determined by adding specific statutory increases and subtracting specific statutory decreases.

Statutory Increases to the Pool: Under paragraph 37(1)(a), the pool is increased by expenditures of a current nature incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada, including: the portion of salary or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED (or undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED under the Traditional Method); the cost of materials consumed (Line 320) or transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED; lease costs of equipment used for SR&ED incurred after December 15, 2024 (Lines 350 and 355); contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant (Line 340 for arm's-length and Line 345 for non-arm's-length); third-party payments to corporations and approved entities (Line 370); and actual overhead and other expenditures when the Traditional Method is used (Line 360). (Under the Proxy Method, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount [PPA] is never added to the Section 37 pool; actual overhead expenditures are deducted as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1)).

Under paragraph 37(1)(b) (restored by Bill C-15), the pool is increased by eligible capital expenditures for depreciable property (other than a building or leasehold interest in a building, except a prescribed special-purpose building under ITR section 2903) acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (Line 390). Under subsection 37(6), claimed capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) are treated as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed to the taxpayer, precluding duplicate CCA claims under paragraph 20(1)(a) and Part XI of the Regulations. Additional statutory increases to the pool include: repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool (paragraph 37(1)(c), Line 445); amounts included in income in a preceding year due to a negative pool balance under paragraph 12(1)(v) (paragraph 37(1)(c.1)); amounts added due to prior-year SR&ED ITC recapture (paragraph 37(1)(c.2)) or partnership ITC recapture excess amounts (paragraph 37(1)(c.3)); and pool balances transferred on an amalgamation or wind-up (Line 452) alongside prior-year pool balances (Line 450). (Note: Under subsection 37(4) and ITR paragraph 2902(c), no deduction is allowed for expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED).

Statutory Decreases to the Pool and Negative Pool Balance Recapture: The pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced by: government or non-government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received at the filing-due date for expenditures included in the pool (paragraph 37(1)(d)); provincial super-allowance benefit amounts (paragraph 37(1)(d.1)); federal SR&ED ITCs applied against tax payable and/or refunded in the preceding taxation year (paragraph 37(1)(e), Line 435); sales of SR&ED capital assets and other deductions (Line 440); amounts deducted from the pool under subsection 37(1) in preceding taxation years (paragraph 37(1)(f)); insolvency deductions under section 61.3 in preceding years (paragraph 37(1)(f.1)); and pool reductions resulting from a loss restriction event under subsection 37(6.1) (paragraph 37(1)(h)).

If the statutory reductions exceed the pool's additions and opening balance—resulting in a negative pool balance at the end of the taxation year—that negative amount must be included directly in the taxpayer's net income for tax purposes in that year under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the Income Tax Act. Because paragraph 37(1)(c.1) adds any amount taxed under paragraph 12(1)(v) back into the pool in the subsequent year, the pool balance at the start of the following taxation year is reset to nil (zero).
3.3 Loss Restriction Events (Subsection 37(6.1)), Related Corporations (Subsection 37(1.1)), and Partnerships
Three specialized corporate structural rules govern the Section 37 pool across corporate groups, M&A transactions, and partnerships:

items: Loss Restriction Events / Acquisition of Control (Subsection 37(6.1) and Paragraph 37(1)(h)): When control of a corporation is acquired (a loss restriction event) or when a trust has a new majority-interest beneficiary, subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h) (amended by Bill C-15 under subparagraph 37(6.1)(a)(i)(B) to include restored capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) made or acquired on or after December 16, 2024) restrict the carryforward of the unused SR&ED deduction pool. Upon a loss restriction event, the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced to nil, and may only be deducted in a subsequent taxation year if the business to which the SR&ED expenditure related is continued for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of the corporation's income for that year (before deducting the SR&ED pool) from that same business or a similar business.

SR&ED Related to a Business of a Related Corporation (Subsection 37(1.1)): Under subsection 37(1.1), when a corporate claimant performs SR&ED that is related to a business actively carried on by a related corporation (for example, where a wholly owned R&D subsidiary performs SR&ED while the parent corporation carries on the commercial business), the SR&ED is considered related to a business of the claimant (determined without reference to control by right).

Partnerships (Paragraph 96(1)(e.1) and Subsection 127(8)): Under paragraph 96(1)(e.1), a partnership cannot carry forward any amount in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period; the entire pool balance must be deducted when computing the partnership's net income or loss for the fiscal period in which the expenditures were incurred. Since a partnership is not a taxpayer, it cannot claim an ITC directly; instead, under subsection 127(8), the ITC is calculated at the partnership level at the 15% basic rate and allocated to eligible partners (limited by each partner's partnership at-risk amount and excluding "specified members" as defined in subsection 248(1)). By contrast, participants in a joint venture file their own separate SR&ED claims for their respective share of work and expenditures.

body.text: 4. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Expenditure Limits, and Refundability Rules
4.1 Basic (15%) Versus Enhanced (35%) Investment Tax Credit Rates

Under subsection 127(5), subsection 127(9), and subsection 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act, the federal SR&ED programme provides two Investment Tax Credit rates applied to a claimant's "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" (Line 570 of Form T661):

items: The Basic ITC Rate (15%): Applies to corporations (other than CCPCs and ECPCs within their expenditure limit), individuals (sole proprietorships), trusts, and partners of a partnership, as well as to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit.

The Enhanced ITC Rate (35%): Under subsection 127(10.1), eligible Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn an additional 20% ITC on top of the 15% basic rate, yielding a total 35% ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit.

body.text: 4.2 Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and the $6 Million Expenditure Limit

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual SR&ED expenditure limit for a CCPC under subsection 127(10.2) is $6,000,000 (doubled from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). Where two or more CCPCs are associated (subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit must be shared among the associated group members and allocated on Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit).

Under the default Taxable Capital Method, a CCPC's expenditure limit is reduced based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation (aggregated with all associated corporations) for the immediately preceding taxation year. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 limit began to decrease when prior-year taxable capital reached $10,000,000 and became nil at $50,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $15,000,000 and becomes nil ($0) starting at $75,000,000.

In addition, under subsection 127(10.32) (enacted by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), a stand-alone CCPC or a group of associated CCPCs (if all associated group members jointly elect on the prescribed form) may elect to calculate its $6,000,000 expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.6) using the Revenue Method (the three-fiscal-year average annual revenue phase-out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000) in the same manner as an ECPC. Where associated CCPCs make this election, the revenue of all corporations associated in the current taxation year must be included across the full three-year lookback period, even if they were not associated during those prior years.
4.3 Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the Three-Year Average Revenue Phase-Out (Subsection 127(10.6))

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(10.1) and subsection 127(10.6) grant Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) access to the enhanced 35% ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Under subsection 127(9), an ECPC is defined as a corporation that, throughout the taxation year, is a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange, is resident in Canada, is not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner by one or more non-resident persons, and would not—if each share of its capital stock owned by a non-resident person (as determined, absent actual knowledge, based on publicly available information including securities law filings before the year) were owned by a single particular person—be controlled by that particular person.

Under subsection 127(10.6), an ECPC's $6,000,000 maximum annual expenditure limit is gradually reduced when its average annual revenue over the preceding three fiscal years exceeds $15,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) starting at $75,000,000. For a non-consolidated ECPC, average annual revenue is calculated over the three fiscal years immediately preceding and ending before the particular taxation year based on its financial statements. For an ECPC that is a member of a consolidated group (defined via "consolidated financial statements" in subsection 127(9) as statements presenting the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of group members as a single economic entity), average annual revenue is calculated over the three fiscal years immediately preceding and ending in the last calendar year that ended before the end of the particular taxation year, as reflected in the consolidated financial statements of the ultimate parent entity. Changes in the size of a consolidated group during the three-year lookback period do not require retroactive adjustments unless reflected in the consolidated financial statements.

Under subsection 127(10.61), the expenditure limit of an ECPC that is a member of a consolidated group at any time in the year is nil unless the group files an election under subsection 127(10.62) to allocate the maximum group expenditure limit among member ECPCs. If a consolidated group fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days of a request by the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister will allocate the limit among the group members under subsection 127(10.63). Under subsection 127(10.64), special rules govern multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year, and for any taxation year shorter than 51 weeks, the expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365 (for example, a $6,000,000 limit for a 273-day short tax year adjusts to $4,487,671).
4.4 Qualifying Corporations (Subsection 127.1(2)), Refundability Rates, Carrybacks, and Carryforwards

Under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 2026), earned SR&ED ITCs must first be applied to reduce federal Part I income tax payable for the year; any remaining unused ITCs are eligible for cash refunds or carryforward/carryback depending on the claimant's classification and whether the expenditures are current or capital.

For both CCPCs (other than "excluded corporations") and ECPCs (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), unused ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate up to the corporation's $6,000,000 expenditure limit are 100% refundable in cash on current expenditures and 40% refundable in cash on eligible capital expenditures (acquired after December 15, 2024).

On qualified SR&ED expenditures in excess of the expenditure limit, all corporations earn ITCs at the 15% basic rate. For ECPCs and non-qualifying CCPCs, this 15% ITC above the expenditure limit is non-refundable. However, if a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2)—meaning a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income (combined with all associated corporations) did not exceed its "qualifying income limit"—the CCPC can obtain a 40% cash refund on the 15% ITC earned on both current and capital expenditures above the expenditure limit. As noted in the CRA Glossary, the qualifying income limit under subsection 127.1(2) begins at $500,000 ($500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) / $40,000,000]) and is reduced when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the associated group passes the statutory threshold ($10 million under legacy rules; updated to $15 million in 2026 tax guides). Unincorporated individuals and certain trusts also receive a 40% cash refund on their 15% basic ITC across both current and capital expenditures.

5. Qualifying Expenditures (Allowable Versus Qualified SR&ED Expenditures)

In Canadian SR&ED compliance, claimants must distinguish between "allowable SR&ED expenditures" (computed in Part 3 of Form T661, which enter the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool) and "qualified SR&ED expenditures" (computed in Part 4 of Form T661, which form the subsection 127(9) base for calculating the Investment Tax Credit).
5.1 Salaries and Wages, Directly Engaged Personnel, the 90% ASA Rule, and Foreign Work (Subsection 37(1.5))

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I (typically reported on a T4 slip). Eligible salary or wages include regular wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips or gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, bonuses (for employees other than specified employees), remuneration based on profits (for employees other than specified employees), employment inducements or non-competition payments, and taxable benefits under section 6 (such as automobile benefits, housing/board/meals, gifts/awards, low-interest loans, group term life insurance, tuition fees, supplementary sick benefits, and employer savings plan contributions). While cash outlays for employee taxable benefits may be included directly in SR&ED salary or wages, non-cash taxable benefits may be included only if the benefit value represents a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes recoverable GST/HST or PST input tax credits, and the actual underlying costs are not claimed separately as a business expense.

Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages explicitly exclude: the employer's share of related benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, or provincial payroll taxes, which may be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method, or are covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method); payments for extended vacation or extended sick leave; stock option benefits under section 7 (considered not to be an expenditure incurred for SR&ED); retiring allowances (which may be considered overhead under the Traditional Method); and unpaid remuneration not paid within 180 days of the tax year-end under subsection 78(4).

Directly Engaged Employees and the All or Substantially All (ASA — 90%) Rule: Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV)), only the portion of salary or wages of employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada may be claimed. Under the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and ITR paragraph 2900(2)(b)), salary or wages of employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED are claimed as SR&ED wages, while salary or wages of clerical and administrative staff (e.g., HR, accounting, finance, purchasing) providing support that is directly related and incremental to SR&ED may be claimed as overhead on Line 360. Whether an employee is "directly engaged" is a question of fact determined by the actual hands-on tasks performed rather than job title, covering tasks under paragraphs (a) to (d) of subsection 248(1): preparing equipment or materials for experiments, conducting tests and analyses, collecting required data, writing computer programs, performing engineering or mathematical analysis, and providing first-line technical supervision that directly guides ongoing SR&ED. Non-technological management functions beyond first-line supervision and clerical/administrative tasks are not directly engaged. Under ITR subsection 2900(5) and ITA subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (B)(IV), when an employee spends all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of their total working time in the taxation year on eligible SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is deemed to be incurred on SR&ED.

Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)): Although general expenditures for R&D carried on outside Canada (subsection 37(2)) cannot be claimed on Form T661 and do not earn ITCs, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) allow a claimant to include a limited amount of "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work performed outside Canada (reported on Line 265, Line 307 [non-specified employees], and Line 309 [specified employees] of Form T661). Under paragraph 37(1.5)(b), permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada are capped at 10% of the total SR&ED salary and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED carried on in Canada during the year.
5.2 Specified Employee Restrictions: The 5x YMPE Cap, 2.5x YMPE Proxy Cap, and Form T1174

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, a "specified employee" is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation (counting shares of persons not dealing at arm's length)—or who otherwise does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, sibling, or other related individual).
Specified employees are governed by four strict statutory limitations across subsections 37(9) to 37(9.5) of the Income Tax Act and subsections 2900(7) to 2900(10) of the Income Tax Regulations:
First, under subsection 37(9), any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid or payable in respect of a specified employee is completely excluded from allowable and qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Second, under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum amount a claimant can claim as an allowable SR&ED expenditure for the salary or wages of a specified employee in a taxation year is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee. Per Government of Canada CPP parameters for the 2026 taxation year, the YMPE is $74,600.00, which sets the maximum allowable SR&ED salary cap at $373,000.00 per specified employee (5 × $74,600).

Third, when calculating the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 (Lines 850 to 858), ITR subsection 2900(7) restricts the includable salary base for each specified employee to the lesser of: (i) the actual SR&ED salary claimed; (ii) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (combining SR&ED and non-SR&ED work, and excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year); or (iii) 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the tax year ends, prorated by the number of days in the tax year that the claimant employed the individual (2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), with no proration for time during the year when the employee was not a specified employee). For the 2026 taxation year, 2.5 × YMPE equals $186,500.00 (2.5 × $74,600).

Fourth, under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.5) and ITR subsections 2900(8) and 2900(10), if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (including related individuals or partnerships with related/associated partners deemed to be associated corporations), both the 5× YMPE expenditure cap and the 2.5× YMPE proxy salary base cap must be shared among the associated corporations. Under subsections 37(9.3) and 37(9.4), associated corporations claiming SR&ED wages for the same specified employee must allocate the cap using prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED), accompanied by a certified copy of the directors' resolution authorizing the agreement (or a sole shareholder's signed confirmation where one shareholder owns 100% of both corporations). Each associated corporation must file Form T1174 no later than its respective 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline; otherwise, the specified employee's salary is statutorily deemed not to be an expenditure on SR&ED.
5.3 Materials Consumed Versus Materials Transformed and the Tangible Object Requirement

Under ITA subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and (B)(V) and ITR paragraph 2900(2)(a), the cost of materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada is an allowable expenditure under both the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method.

Per the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, an item qualifies as a material for SR&ED only if it satisfies the Tangible Object Requirement: "materials for SR&ED" refers to raw materials, substances, or other items that are physical and tangible (existing in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and that, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a tangible object ("thing") on which the SR&ED is being carried out, or a tangible object that results from the SR&ED being carried out. Materials can be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, but their cost can only be claimed in the specific taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—not when purchased and placed into inventory. For purchased items, "cost" means laid-down cost (invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, storage, and other acquisition costs); for internally manufactured inventory, cost includes laid-down material cost plus direct labour and a properly chargeable share of production overhead (even under the Proxy Method). Under subsection 127(11.6), for materials purchased from a non-arm's-length supplier, the SR&ED ITC is restricted to the cost incurred by the non-arm's-length supplier, excluding any intercompany profit element (Line 543 of Form T661).

body.text: 5.4 Arm's-Length Subcontractors (80% Rule), Non-Arm's-Length Contracts (Form T1146), and Third-Party Payments (Form T1263)

When a claimant engages external entities to perform SR&ED in Canada, the Income Tax Act distinguishes among arm's-length SR&ED contracts, non-arm's-length (NAL) SR&ED contracts, and third-party payments.

Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (ITA Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and Subsection 127(9) — Line 340): An SR&ED contract occurs where a contractor performs SR&ED in Canada on behalf of the claimant, meaning the payer controls the work, assumes the risk, and retains exclusive ownership rights to the SR&ED results. Where a contract includes both SR&ED and non-SR&ED work, the cost must be reasonably allocated so only the SR&ED portion is claimed. If a payer contracts out only support work (paragraph 248(1)(d)) to an arm's-length contractor, the payer can claim the contract amount provided the support work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of core SR&ED performed in Canada by or on behalf of the payer (whereas the arm's-length contractor cannot claim SR&ED for stand-alone support work, and must reduce any SR&ED claim of its own by contract payments received from a Canadian taxable supplier). Under subsection 18(9), any payment for contracted SR&ED not yet performed is a prepaid expense and is non-deductible until the year the services are rendered. To qualify for an ITC, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" under subsection 127(9) (payments to non-taxable suppliers are deducted on Line 528). While 100% of an arm's-length SR&ED contract enters the Section 37 deductible pool (Line 340), paragraph (a)(ii) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) limits the ITC base to 80% of the contract expenditure (implemented by deducting 20% on Line 529 of Form T661). Crucially, consequential to restoring capital expenditures, Bill C-15 repealed former subsection 37(14) (the capital look-through rule that previously required reducing contractor claims by the contractor's capital or lease costs) for property acquired and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Subsection 127(9) Paragraph (f) and Subsection 127(13) — Line 345): Where a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer (section 251), 100% of the expenditure is allowable in the payer's Section 37 deduction pool (Line 345), but it is excluded from qualified expenditures (paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9)) and earns 0% ITC for the payer. Instead, the payment is not treated as a "contract payment" to the NAL performer, enabling the NAL performer to claim the SR&ED ITC directly on its own underlying costs (including support work performed for the NAL payer). Alternatively, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and NAL payer may jointly file prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures (capped at the contract amount) to the payer (Line 508 and Line 546 of Form T661). Under subsection 127(24), anti-avoidance rules prevent circumventing NAL rules by inserting an arm's-length intermediary between a payer and an NAL performer.

Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) — Line 370 and Form T1263): Unlike an SR&ED contract (where the payer controls the work and owns exclusive rights), a third-party payment occurs when a claimant makes a payment to an approved entity—such as an approved association, university, college, research institute, granting council, non-profit SR&ED corporation, or resident corporation—where the performer controls the SR&ED work, the SR&ED is carried on in Canada and relates to a business of the claimant, and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED. Third-party payments are claimed in the year paid, are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 80% eligible for Section 127 ITCs (with 20% deducted on Line 529), and require attaching a completed Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment.
5.5 Overhead Methodologies: The 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (ITR Section 2900) Versus the Traditional Method and Cloud Computing

Under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must elect annually on Lines 160 and 162 of Form T661 to compute SR&ED overhead using either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. The election is irrevocable for the taxation year once filed, and if no method is selected on Form T661, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method by default.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or claim actual overhead expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661 and includes it in qualified expenditures on Line 502 in Part 4. Under ITR subsection 2900(4) (Line 820 of Form T661), the PPA is 55% of the claimant's eligible salary base. (Audit Warning: The proxy rate was 65% for 2012 and prior years, 60% for 2013, and has been 55% since 2014; using 65% overstates the credit and will be corrected on assessment). Under ITR subsections 2900(7) to 2900(9), the salary base comprises the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits (Line 812), prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year (Line 310), employer-paid related benefits, and specified employee wages above the lesser of 75% of total salary or 2.5× YMPE. Furthermore, ITR subsection 2900(6) imposes an overall cap on the PPA (A − B − C, where A is total business deductions claimed in computing net income including cost of goods sold, B is deductions under Sections 20, 24, 26, 30, 32, 37, 66–66.8, and 104, and C is expenditures for the use of or right to use a building) so that total claimed SR&ED and PPA amounts cannot exceed total business expenses. The PPA earns an SR&ED ITC on Line 502, but is never added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool because the underlying actual overhead expenses (general purpose office equipment or furniture, clerical/support staff wages, office supplies, utilities) are deducted as ordinary business expenses.

Under the Traditional Method (ITR subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)), the claimant tracks and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661, which enter both the Section 37 deductible pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures at 100%. Per ITR paragraph 2900(2)(c) and the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, an overhead expenditure qualifies only if it meets two mandatory tests: (1) the Directly Related Test, requiring a direct causal linkage (with no intervening step or intermediary) between the expenditure and the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED (secondary overhead is disallowed); and (2) the Incremental Test, requiring that the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada not occurred (disallowing fixed-cost maintenance contracts and post-project waste disposal). Allowable Traditional Method overhead includes the employer's share of related benefits for hands-on SR&ED staff; clerical/administrative wages directly related and incremental to ongoing SR&ED; non-SR&ED contract work (electricians, welders, mechanics) directly related and incremental to SR&ED; retiring allowances and relocation expenses for SR&ED personnel; incremental utilities; travel and training in Canada; and clinical trial volunteer fees.

body.text: 5.6 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), Equipment Leases, and Special-Purpose Buildings

Enacted by Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the restoration of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs applies to depreciable property acquired (and available for use under subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), and to lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024. Capital and lease expenditures made after 2013 and before December 16, 2024 remain ineligible.

SR&ED Capital Expenditures — All or Substantially All (ASA ≥90%) Test (ITA Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) & (B)(III)): Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire new or used depreciable property (other than a building or leasehold interest in a building) after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure (Line 390 of Form T661, with the top 10 items per project listed on Line 262 and the top 20 overall in Part 6B Box 780) if at the time of acquisition the claimant intends either: (1) to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; or (2) to consume ASA (90% or more) of the property's value in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Capital cost includes invoice price, legal, accounting, engineering, installation, customs/excise duties, and transportation/storage fees (or material, labour, and overhead excluding profit if self-manufactured). While both new and used ASA depreciable property enter the Section 37 deductible pool, ITR paragraph 2902(b) prescribes that used equipment is disallowed for Section 127 ITC purposes and must be deducted on Line 532 of Form T661.

Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE — Primarily >50% to <90% SR&ED Use) (Subsection 127(9) Paragraph (a)(iii)): Under the CRA's Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA test may qualify for an SR&ED ITC as Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) (Line 504 and Part 6C of Form T661) if it is new, is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under ITR subsection 2900(11) (property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes), is not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and is used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada. SUE capital cost is not added to the Section 37 pool (instead, regular CCA is claimed on Schedule T2SCH8). For ITC purposes, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost (computed without borrowed money costs under section 21 or deemed capital costs under subsection 13(7.4), and adjusted for non-arm's-length costs under subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies in the "first period" (ending at the end of the first tax year occurring at least 12 months after acquisition) as first term shared-use-equipment, and an additional 25% (1/4) qualifies in the "second period" (at least 24 months after acquisition) as second term shared-use-equipment, totalling 50% of capital cost.

Equipment Lease Costs (Incurred After December 15, 2024): Current expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, for leasing equipment used in SR&ED in Canada are claimed on Lines 350 and 355 in Part 3 and Part 6A Box 759 of Form T661. Under the Proxy Method, lease costs for GPOEF are excluded, whereas under the Traditional Method, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of operating time may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures.

Exclusion of Buildings and the Prescribed Special-Purpose Building Exception (ITA Paragraphs 37(8)(d)–(e) and ITR Section 2903): Under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and 37(8)(e), capital or lease expenditures for a building or leasehold interest in a building (including mobile homes or portable shelters affixed to a permanent foundation, though excluding tents, canvas marquees, air-supported fabric domes, or non-building structures like bridges or transmission towers) are excluded from SR&ED. The sole exceptions for property acquired after December 15, 2024, are: (1) third-party payments enabling an arm's-length approved research institute/association or an approved university/college (where the payer acquires no interest in the building) to acquire a building; and (2) prescribed special-purpose buildings under ITR section 2903, which must have working areas designed and constructed to have a physical displacement in any direction of not more than 0.02 micrometres, and an interior airspace containing, per 0.028 cubic metres, fewer than 350 airborne particles ≤0.1 µm (and zero >0.1 µm), fewer than 75 airborne particles ≤0.2 µm (and zero >0.2 µm), fewer than 30 airborne particles ≤0.3 µm (and zero >0.3 µm), or fewer than 10 airborne particles ≤0.5 µm (and zero >0.5 µm).
5.7 Investment Tax Credit Recapture Rules (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, SR&ED ITC recapture ensures that only net SR&ED costs attract tax credits by adding an amount back to a claimant's Part I tax payable when SR&ED property is sold or converted to commercial use.

Recapture is triggered when all four statutory conditions are present: (1) the claimant acquired the property in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36)); (2) the cost of the property was claimed as a qualified SR&ED expenditure (such as materials transformed, SR&ED capital expenditures acquired before 2014 or after December 15, 2024, Shared-Use-Equipment, or property acquired under an arm's-length SR&ED contract); (3) a percentage of the property's cost was included in computing the claimant's SR&ED ITC; and (4) in the current taxation year, the claimant disposes of or converts to commercial use the property (or another property incorporating it).

When triggered, recapture is calculated using the proceeds of disposition (or Fair Market Value upon commercial conversion or non-arm's-length transfer) and the rate at which the original ITC was generated on the property, and is added directly to tax payable for the year. In the following taxation year, the recaptured ITC amount is added back to the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3). Under subsection 127(32), internal salaries, wages, and overhead are never subject to recapture ("cost" cannot exceed the amount paid to acquire the property from another person), nor does disposing of intellectual property (IP) trigger recapture unless it incorporates purchased physical property claimed as an SR&ED expenditure. Furthermore, under the CRA's 10% de minimis rule, no recapture applies if proceeds from a scrap sale or the FMV upon commercial conversion are less than 10% of the total cost of the property. Under subsections 127(33) to 127(35), transferring SR&ED capital property to a non-arm's-length purchaser who continues to use it all or substantially all (ASA) for SR&ED defers recapture until the purchaser subsequently disposes of or converts the property.
6. Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Grant Stacking
6.1 Accrual Recognition and Project-by-Project Reductions (Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(18) to 127(20))

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) (for the Section 37 deductible pool) and subsections 127(18) to 127(20) (for Section 127 qualified expenditures), SR&ED claims must be reduced by all government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments.

Under subsection 127(9) and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (updated March 27, 2026), government assistance means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—excluding the federal SR&ED ITC. It includes funding from foreign governments, Crown corporations, public authorities, indirect assistance channeled through government-funded non-profit entities, and non-commercial or conditional repayable contributions. Non-government assistance means any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (read without reference to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)). A contract payment is an amount paid or payable by an arm's-length taxable supplier for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of a person or partnership entitled to a deduction under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) or (i.1), or an amount payable by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity under section 149 for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf.

Assistance and contract payments are recognized on an accrual basis in the taxation year in which the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive the amount on or before the filing-due date. Reductions are applied on a project-by-project basis: for the Section 37 pool, excess assistance over a project's expenditures reduces the project pool to nil and is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x); for Section 127 qualified expenditures, excess assistance is carried forward under subsection 127(18) to reduce future qualified expenditures on that project. Under subsections 127(19) and 127(20), when assistance received by one member of a non-arm's-length group exceeds its expenditures on a joint project, the excess is allocated among the related group members using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, reported on Line 540 of Form T661). When a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED claim, the repayment increases the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) (Line 445) and earns an ITC on Line 560 at the rate that applied when the original assistance reduced the claim.
6.2 Stacking Mechanics with NRC-IRAP, Global Innovation Clusters, and the Strategic Innovation Fund

Canadian businesses frequently combine direct federal R&D grants with SR&ED tax credits. As noted in Canadian innovation funding guides, total government assistance across stacked programmes (grants plus tax credits) is generally capped at 75% of eligible project costs.

body.text: 6.3 Interaction Between Provincial R&D Tax Credits, Federal SR&ED Pools, and the Prescribed Proxy Amount

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act and Section 4.5 of the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (such as Ontario's OITC and ORDTC, Quebec's CRIC, BC's SR&ED credit, Alberta's IEG, and Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Atlantic, and Yukon credits) are treated as government assistance.

Consequently, earning a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit reduces the claimant's current-year federal qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18) regardless of whether the claimant uses the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method, and regardless of whether the provincial credit is refundable or non-refundable. However, for the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, the treatment depends on the overhead method elected. Under the Traditional Method, the entire provincial R&D tax credit reduces the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d). Under the Proxy Method, the portion of the provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that relates to the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) does not reduce the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (because the PPA is not included in the Section 37 pool); instead, that PPA-related portion of the provincial tax credit must be included directly in income in the year it is received under paragraph 12(1)(x). If a corporation wishes to prevent a non-refundable provincial R&D credit from reducing its federal SR&ED pool and 35% refundable ITC, it must formally renounce or waive the provincial credit on or before the filing-due date of its income tax return (6 months after tax year-end).
6.4 Comprehensive Worked Numerical Modelling of Federal-Provincial-Grant Stacking

To demonstrate the exact statutory mechanics of stacking direct grants, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount, provincial R&D tax credits, and the federal SR&ED ITC, consider two calculations for a CCPC in its 2026 taxation year (within the $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit) electing the Proxy Method:
Scenario A: Ontario CCPC Claiming NRC-IRAP + Ontario OITC + Ontario ORDTC + Federal SR&ED
Assume an Ontario CCPC incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries in Ontario (non-specified employees, no bonuses) and receives a $400,000 non-repayable NRC-IRAP salary grant:

items: Gross Allowable Salary Expenditure: $1,000,000.

Prescribed Proxy Amount — 55% PPA (Line 502): Under ITR subsection 2900(4), the 55% PPA is calculated on the $1,000,000 salary base before deducting the IRAP grant (55% × $1,000,000), yielding $550,000.
Gross Qualified Expenditures Before Assistance: $1,000,000 (Salary) + $550,000 (PPA) = $1,550,000.
Less: NRC-IRAP Government Assistance: $1,550,000 − $400,000 = $1,150,000 net qualified Ontario expenditures.
Step 1 Provincial Credit — Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — 8% Refundable on Schedule 566): Calculated on the $1,150,000 net qualified expenditure base: 8% × $1,150,000 = $92,000 cash refund.

Step 2 Provincial Credit — Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — 3.5% Non-Refundable on Schedule 508): Because the OITC is government assistance that reduces eligible expenditures for the ORDTC, the ORDTC base is $1,150,000 − $92,000 = $1,058,000. The ORDTC earned is 3.5% × $1,058,000 = $37,030.

Federal Qualified SR&ED Expenditures After Provincial Credits (Line 570): Subtract both the OITC ($92,000) and ORDTC ($37,030) from the $1,150,000 base under subsection 127(18): $1,150,000 − $92,000 − $37,030 = $1,020,970.
Federal Enhanced SR&ED ITC (35% Refundable on Schedule T2SCH31): 35% × $1,020,970 = $357,339.50 cash refund.

Total Combined Recovery on $1,000,000 Cash Outlay: $400,000 (IRAP) + $92,000 (OITC) + $37,030 (ORDTC) + $357,339.50 (Federal SR&ED) = $886,369.50 (88.64% of the $1,000,000 payroll outlay; or if no IRAP grant was received, $124,000 OITC + $49,910 ORDTC + $481,631.50 Federal SR&ED = $655,541.50, representing a 65.55% combined tax credit recovery on $1,000,000 of Ontario SR&ED salaries).
