Assume a Quebec CCPC in its 2026 taxation year incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries in Quebec across 10 full-time (100% SR&ED) engineers ($100,000 salary each) and acquires $200,000 of new ASA (100% SR&ED) testing equipment in Quebec after December 15, 2024 (no grants received, electing the federal Proxy Method):

items: Gross Quebec CRIC Qualified Expenditures: $1,000,000 (Salaries) + $200,000 (Capital Equipment) = $1,200,000.

Quebec CRIC Exclusion Threshold (2026): The greater of $50,000 or the sum of the 2026 Quebec Basic Personal Amount ($18,952 per advisory guides) per employee prorated by SR&ED time: 10 employees × $18,952 × 100% = $189,520.
Net CRIC Base Above Exclusion Threshold: $1,200,000 − $189,520 = $1,010,480.

Quebec CRIC Refundable Credit Calculation (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T): The first $1,000,000 above the threshold earns 30% ($300,000), and the remaining $10,480 earns 20% ($2,096), yielding a Total Refundable Quebec CRIC of $302,096 (allocable pro rata: 5/6 or $251,746.67 to current salaries, and 1/6 or $50,349.33 to capital equipment).

Federal Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Form T661): Current qualified expenditures equal $1,000,000 (Salaries) + $550,000 (55% PPA) − $251,746.67 (CRIC on salaries) = $1,298,253.33, while capital qualified expenditures equal $200,000 (Equipment) − $50,349.33 (CRIC on equipment) = $149,650.67.

Federal Enhanced SR&ED ITC (35% Rate): The current ITC is 35% × $1,298,253.33 = $454,388.67 (100% refundable in cash), and the capital ITC is 35% × $149,650.67 = $52,377.73 (of which 40% = $20,951.09 is refunded in cash, and 60% = $31,426.64 offsets federal Part I tax or carries forward 20 years).

Total Combined Federal + Quebec Recovery on $1,200,000 Outlay: $302,096 (CRIC) + $454,388.67 (Fed Current ITC) + $52,377.73 (Fed Capital ITC) = $808,862.40 (67.41% of total cash outlay, with $777,435.76 received as an immediate cash refund).

body.text: 7. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes
7.1 Quebec: Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC — Form RD-1029.8.CR-T)

For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec's Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation – Codes 112 and 113, introduced in Quebec Finance Bulletin 2025-6) consolidates and replaces eight legacy provincial R&D tax credits, including the discontinued forms RD-1029.7 (Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D)), RD-1029.8.6 (Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium), RD-1029.8.9.03 (Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium), and RD-1029.8.16.1 (Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research). (Quebec's separate R&D deduction calculation continues to use Form RD-222).

To qualify for the CRIC, a corporation must operate a business in Quebec, maintain an establishment in Quebec, and undertake eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Quebec (or cause them to be undertaken on its behalf in Quebec under contract). The CRIC covers two distinct activity streams: (1) eligible R&D activities (basic research, applied research, and experimental development, harmonized with the federal definition in ITA subsection 248(1) and scientifically reviewed by the CRA); and (2) eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in conjunction with (as a continuation of) R&D work carried out in Quebec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization work includes tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation (including quality control only if related to implementing a quality control system needed for initial approval/certification), and product design, including developing form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials (with advisory guides noting coverage of competitive analysis of operational constraints, prototype development, pilot user validation, and usage scenarios).

Qualified CRIC expenditures incurred in Quebec comprise: 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees for eligible work; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for an eligible contract carried out in Quebec; 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity (defined in section 1029.8 of the Taxation Act (Quebec)); and 100% of property acquisition costs (depreciable capital equipment used in the eligible work, excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings, and excluding property used under a large investment project tax holiday certificate). Qualified expenditures must first exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the applicable Basic Personal Amount (BPA) of the personal income tax system (reported by tax advisory guides as $18,571 for 2025 and $18,952 for 2026) for each employee, adjusted to reflect the percentage of time spent by that employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

Above the exclusion threshold, the CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit to all eligible corporations (CCPCs, public corporations, and foreign subsidiaries alike, with no corporate asset test) at a rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures (allocated among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T) and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000. An expenditure claimed under the CRIC cannot be combined with another Quebec tax credit (such as the C3i investment and innovation tax credit) on the same expense. Corporations claim the CRIC by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (along with RD-1029.8.EN-T and RD-1029.8.PR-T, as applicable) with their Quebec corporate income tax return.
7.2 Ontario: OITC (Schedule 566), ORDTC (Schedule 508), and OBRITC (Schedules 568 and 569)

Ontario provides three corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA. When federal Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, Ontario automatically harmonized with the federal restoration of capital expenditures for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, across both the OITC and ORDTC.

The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007, Schedule 566 / T2SCH566) provides qualifying corporations with an 8% fully refundable tax credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum annual credit of $240,000, shared among associated corporations and prorated for short tax years). The $3,000,000 expenditure limit phases out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year federal taxable income, or between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable paid-up capital. Qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024.

The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 45 of the Taxation Act, 2007, Schedule 508 / T2SCH508 and Schedule T2SCH31) provides all corporations having a permanent establishment in Ontario with a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (including 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024), with no expenditure limit. The 8% OITC is government assistance that reduces the eligible expenditure base for the 3.5% ORDTC. Unused ORDTC can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, or waived in writing within 6 months of tax year-end; recapture is calculated using the statutory 23.56% rate.

The Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007, Schedules 568 and 569 / T2SCH568 and T2SCH569) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified current expenditures incurred under an eligible SR&ED contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) in Ontario (such as an Ontario university, community college, hospital research institute, or designated non-profit organization), capped at $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures annually (maximum annual refundable credit of $4,000,000). The corporation must not be "connected" to the ERI (for example, the ERI cannot own shares carrying >10% of voting rights or >10% of fair market value of all issued shares of the corporation).
7.3 British Columbia: BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666)

Governed by Sections 97 to 103 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia) and administered by the CRA, the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit is claimed on Form T666 no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year by corporations with a permanent establishment in BC (including active corporate members of a partnership, but excluding individuals and employee venture capital corporations). Qualifying CCPCs earn a 10% fully refundable tax credit on qualified BC SR&ED expenditures up to their expenditure limit as defined in the federal Income Tax Act. Following the amendments in BC Budget 2026 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the refundable credit is available to both CCPCs and ECPCs on up to $6,000,000 of qualified BC SR&ED expenditures (maximum annual refund of $600,000, shared among associated corporations; previously $3,000,000 and $300,000), the expenditure limit begins to phase out at $15,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and is eliminated at $75,000,000, capital expenditures are again eligible, and the credit no longer has an expiry date. Other corporations, and CCPCs and ECPCs on expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit, earn a 10% non-refundable tax credit that can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 10 years to reduce BC corporate tax payable, or renounced. Recapture applies if property is disposed of or converted to commercial use within 10 years of acquisition.
7.4 Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970)

Governed by Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (and Information Circular IEG-1) and administered by the Province of Alberta through its corporate tax system, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) is a fully refundable grant claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970. The IEG provides an 8% base payment on eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's base level of spending (calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years), and an enhanced 20% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the 2-year average base spending level.

The IEG applies to a maximum of $4,000,000 in annual R&D spending and phases out incrementally for corporations (and associated groups) with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, becoming nil at $50,000,000. Crucially, unlike the federal and Ontario regimes, eligible expenditures for the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant explicitly exclude capital expenditures made after December 15, 2024. The filing deadline for the IEG is 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing-due date, and recapture applies.
7.5 Prairie and Atlantic Provinces and Yukon: Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon

In the Prairie region, Saskatchewan (The Income Tax Act (Saskatchewan), Sections 63 to 63.4 — Form T2SCH403, administered by the CRA) provides non-tax-exempt CCPCs with a 10% refundable tax credit on eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures up to an annual limit of $1,000,000 (maximum $100,000 refund) and a 10% non-refundable credit on expenditures exceeding $1,000,000; other corporations earn a 10% non-refundable credit on all eligible expenditures, with non-refundable credits carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years. Manitoba (The Income Tax Act (Manitoba), Section 7.3 — Schedule T2SCH380, administered by the CRA with a filing deadline of 1 year after the filing-due date) provides a 15% tax credit on eligible Manitoba SR&ED expenditures. For in-house R&D, one-half (7.5%) is refundable and one-half (7.5%) is non-refundable (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years; may be renounced), whereas R&D carried on in Manitoba under contract with a qualifying educational institution is 100% refundable (15%).

In Atlantic Canada and the North, New Brunswick (New Brunswick Income Tax Act, Section 59 — Schedule T2SCH360), Nova Scotia (Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia), Section 41 — Schedule T2SCH340, 18-month filing deadline), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador), Section 42 — Schedule T2SCH301 for corporations and Form T1129 for individuals, filing deadline 12 months after filing-due date) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit administered by the CRA with no expenditure cap. Uniquely, Newfoundland and Labrador does not reduce its eligible expenditure base by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits), and does not apply provincial recapture. Yukon (Income Tax Act (Yukon), Section 15 — Schedule T2SCH442 for corporations and Form T1232 for individuals, administered by the CRA) provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit on eligible Yukon expenditures plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University. Prince Edward Island, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit.

body.text: 8. Governing Bodies, Filing Deadlines, Prescribed Forms, and Claim Preparer Penalties
8.1 The Strict 18-Month Reporting Deadline (Subsection 37(11) and Paragraph 127(9)(m)) and Subsection 220(2.2) Bar

Under subsection 37(11) (for the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for the Section 127 ITC), a claimant must file the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations, or Form T2038(IND) for individuals and trusts) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year.

Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date is generally 6 months after its taxation year-end, a corporation's SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (while unincorporated individuals have 17.5 months after year-end). Per the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, if a corporation's tax year ends on the last day of a month (e.g., February 28), its filing-due date is August 31 of that year and its SR&ED reporting deadline is August 31 of the following year; if a tax year ends on a specific day other than the last day of a month (e.g., January 6), its filing-due date is July 6 and its SR&ED reporting deadline is July 6 of the following year.

Under subsection 37(11.1) and paragraph 127(9)(m), if the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information are filed after the SR&ED reporting deadline, the expenditures are not considered SR&ED expenditures and no ITC is earned. (If Form T661 is filed on time but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the 18-month reporting deadline, the claimant can still deduct the allowable expenditures in the Section 37 pool, but is barred from earning any ITC on those expenditures). Crucially, subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act bars any discretionary extension of the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline.
8.2 The 180-Day Unpaid Amounts Rule (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26))

Two statutory provisions govern accrued SR&ED expenditures that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year. First, under subsection 78(4), any salary or wages incurred in the taxation year that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year (subtracted on Line 315 of Form T661), and instead may be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (though excluded from that later year's 55% PPA salary base under ITR subsection 2900(9)).

Second, under subsection 127(26) and the CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (updated May 22, 2026), an unpaid current expenditure other than salary or wages (such as an arm's-length SR&ED contract on Line 340) is deemed not to have been incurred in the taxation year for ITC purposes if it remains unpaid 180 days after the tax year-end (Line 520 of Form T661). For an unpaid arm's-length contract (e.g., $100,000), two deductions are made on Form T661 in the year incurred: the contract is reduced by 20% ($20,000) on Line 529, and the remaining 80% ($80,000) is deducted as an unpaid expenditure on Line 520. When paid in a subsequent year, only the 80% ($80,000) identified amount is added back to qualified expenditures on Line 500. Crucially, if an unpaid amount is not explicitly identified on Form T661 within the 18-month reporting deadline for the year incurred, it is permanently excluded from total qualified SR&ED expenditures even after it is paid in a subsequent year.
8.3 Line-by-Line Architecture of Form T661 (2026 Revision) and Mandatory Schedules

To claim federal SR&ED incentives, claimants must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 2026) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)).

body.text: 8.4 Part 9 Claim Preparer Disclosures and Joint and Several Liability Under Subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3)

Under paragraph 37(11)(b) and subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) of the Income Tax Act, Part 9 (Lines 935 to 975) of Form T661 requires full disclosure of every "claim preparer"—defined as any person or partnership that has accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED form, excluding an employee who prepares or assists in preparing the form as part of their regular employment duties.

If a claim preparer was engaged (Line 935, Box 1), the claimant must report the preparer's name (Line 940), 15-character Business Number or GST/HST number (Line 945), billing arrangement code (Line 950, such as Code 1 for a contingency fee based on a percentage of the ITC earned, using separate lines for mixed or variable-rate arrangements), numerical billing rate (Line 955, e.g., 15.5 for 15.5% or 75 for $75/hour), description of any other billing arrangement in 10 words or less (Line 960), total fee paid, payable, or expected to be paid (Line 965), and the certifying officer's name, signature, and date (Lines 970 and 975; if no claim preparer was engaged, Box 2 is checked on Line 935 and only Lines 970 and 975 are completed).

Under subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3), if prescribed information about the claim preparer(s) and billing arrangement(s) in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty applies for each SR&ED claim, and the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable for the $1,000 penalty. However, Part 9 information is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, and missing or inaccurate Part 9 information does not disallow the underlying SR&ED claim.
9. CRA Audit Protocols, Pre-Claim Approval, and Dispute Resolution
9.1 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and Processing Service Standards

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process alongside upgrades to the SR&ED Client Portal and the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool. Through My Business Account, eligible businesses can submit an application prior to starting work or incurring costs to determine whether planned projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives, supported by individual one-on-one sessions and webinars, with the CRA providing formal eligibility determinations within 8 weeks.

For post-year-end SR&ED claims filed with a tax return, the CRA's official service standard for processing refundable SR&ED claims selected for review is 180 calendar days from the date the CRA receives a complete claim (which the CRA commits to meeting 90% of the time), while there is no service standard for processing non-refundable SR&ED claims selected for review. (Industry funding guides note that unreviewed refundable federal claims typically process in 60 to 120 days, and clean Quebec CRIC refunds typically process in 60 to 90 days).
9.2 Coordinated Technical and Financial Reviews: Roles of the RTA and FR and SR&ED Review Report (SRR) Codes

Across the CRA's 7 Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs) (which manage files via the CORTAX and RAPID systems), files selected for audit undergo a Coordinated Review conducted cooperatively by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and a Financial Reviewer (FR).

The RTA conducts the Technical Review (recorded in the TF98 file and T2020 log), examining technical documentation, conducting on-site or virtual interviews with the personnel best able to explain the work, touring facilities, evaluating whether the work meets the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1), and issuing the SR&ED Review Report (SRR). In Section 5.1 of the SRR, the RTA records the eligibility determination for each project using five standardized codes: AW (all reviewed work meets the definition of SR&ED); SW (some reviewed work meets the definition of SR&ED and some does not); NW (no claimed work meets the definition of SR&ED); UN (unsubstantiated — claimed work cannot be substantiated to determine if it meets the definition of SR&ED); and AAF (accepted as filed without a review to determine eligibility, which neither confirms nor refutes eligibility).

The FR conducts the Financial Review based on the RTA's technical determinations and the requirements of the Income Tax Act, formulating a written review plan based on risk-grid scoring, examining financial and source documentation (receipts, contracts, payroll records), coordinating with the RTA on joint technical-financial issues, and issuing the proposal letter package (which encloses the RTA's SRR and grants the claimant—generally 30 days—to submit written representations before a final letter and Notice of Assessment or Reassessment are issued).
9.3 Contemporaneous Documentation Standards and Audit Defence Protocols

Under the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives and The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, claimants must maintain supporting evidence generated as the work progresses conveying what work was done, who was involved, when they did the work, and how expenditures were determined. While reviewers consider oral statements made during interviews alongside supporting documentation, the CRA's guide notes that oral statements are not a substitute for keeping adequate documentation or other evidence. Relevant contemporaneous technical and financial records include planning documents, design of experiments (DOE) and experimentation plans, project records, laboratory notebooks, records of trial runs, test protocols, test data, results, analysis and conclusions, dated timesheets, and source documents such as receipts, contracts, and general correspondence.
9.4 Four-Tiered Administrative Escalation, Notices of Objection, and Tax Court of Canada Procedures

When a claimant disagrees with review findings, the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns (Application Policy SR&ED 2000-02R) and the Income Tax Act establish a four-step dispute resolution and legal appeal framework:

items: Step 1 — Talk to the Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and/or Financial Reviewer (FR): Raise concerns directly with the reviewers during the review or within the 30-day written representation window following the proposal letter package and SR&ED Review Report.

Step 2 — Escalate to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM): If discussions with the RTA or FR do not resolve the issue, contact their respective managers (whose contact details are provided in the CRA's initial letter).

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review by the CTSO Assistant Director: Before the file is closed, the claimant may request an Administrative Review by the Assistant Director, who determines whether: (i) the claimant was given due process; and (ii) the technical and financial reviews were consistent with current SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures. The Assistant Director issues an outcome of either Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered (where another person not involved in the original review may conduct a reconsideration).

Step 4 — Formal CRA Objection Process and Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada: Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, where an independent Appeals Officer issues a written decision and either a Notice of Confirmation or a Notice of Reassessment. If unsatisfied, the claimant may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada under either the Informal Procedure (for income tax/ITC amounts up to $25,000, or where the claimant agrees to limit the settlement/dispute amount to $25,000) or the General Procedure (for amounts of any size, requiring formal legal steps and strict rules governing expert witness evidence), with further appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal.

body.text: 10. Foundational Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Judicial Precedents
10.1 The Bedrock Five-Part Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), Justice Donald Bowman articulated the foundational five-criterion legal test for determining whether claimed work qualifies as SR&ED under Canadian law:

items: Technical Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technical risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?

Accordance with the Scientific Method: Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?
Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a scientific or a technological advancement—that is to say, an advancement in the general understanding?
Detailed Record Kept as Work Progresses: Did the taxpayer keep a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed?

body.text: 10.2 Purposive Statutory Interpretation and Appellate Endorsement: Consoltex (1997), RIS-Christie (1998), C.W. Agencies (2001), and Jentel Manufacturing (2011)

In Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 D.T.C. 724 (TCC) (decided March 4, 1997), Justice Bowman established that the SR&ED provisions of the Income Tax Act are aimed at encouraging scientific research in Canada and must be interpreted purposively to give effect to that incentive goal. Subsequently, in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 5087, 235 N.R. 258 (FCA) (1998), the Federal Court of Appeal explicitly endorsed Justice Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic approach for determining whether a project qualifies as SR&ED.

In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, the Federal Court of Appeal summarized and reaffirmed the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria (as approved in RIS-Christie) as the governing standard for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED. A decade later, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355, both the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed once again that the criteria for determining whether work qualifies as SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act are those set out in Northwest Hydraulic.
10.3 Evidentiary Nuances and Contemporaneous Records: 116736 Canada Inc. (1998) and Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. (2014)

In 116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada, [1998] A.C.I. No. 478 (QL) (TCC), Justice Archambault explained that while contemporary reports showing detailed records of each experiment are potentially very important evidence and any taxpayer attempting to convince the Minister or the Court without such evidence places itself in a "very precarious position", neither the Income Tax Act nor the Regulations require that written reports be produced to qualify for the deduction of R&D expenditures; a taxpayer may adduce evidence by way of credible oral testimony.

In Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, Justice Jorré allowed the taxpayer's appeal across four projects and quoted 116736 Canada Inc. with approval, holding that while the existence and content of contemporaneous documents are relevant to determining questions of fact, the existence of contemporaneous documentation is not a legal condition for SR&ED to be recognized, as taxpayers cannot be required in tax matters to do more than the obligations the Income Tax Act imposes on them. Justice Jorré also admonished a CRA scientific adviser testifying as an expert witness in Court for confusing his audit role (where he is guided by CRA administrative guidelines and proof standards) with his role as an expert witness before the Tax Court (which requires an independent opinion based on personal expertise rather than CRA policy manuals).
10.4 Modern Appellate Continuity and Expert Evidence: Kam-Press Metal Products (2021) and National R&D Inc. (2022)

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, the corporate taxpayer appealed the denial of its 2009 and 2010 SR&ED claims, arguing that Northwest Hydraulic should be overturned because the words "scientific method" do not appear explicitly in the text of subsection 248(1). The Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the courts' role is to interpret and elaborate on the meaning of Income Tax Act provisions through a textual, contextual, and purposive interpretation as Justice Bowman did in Northwest Hydraulic, and noting that Northwest Hydraulic had been repeatedly affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie (1998), C.W. Agencies (2001), Jentel Manufacturing (2011), and R&D Pro-innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016).

In National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2020 TCC 47, aff'd 2022 FCA 72, involving software development SR&ED claims where the Tax Court found technological uncertainty existed but the remaining Northwest Hydraulic criteria were not met, the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the Northwest Hydraulic common-law test (applied flexibly in a manner suitable for applied sciences and the taxpayer's business environment). Crucially, the FCA explicitly rejected the taxpayer's argument that the CRA's 2021 SR&ED eligibility guidelines ("Why and How") removed the requirement to follow the scientific method. The FCA also upheld the Tax Court's ruling that the taxpayer's expert report was inadmissible, contrasting cases where an expert improperly opines on the ultimate legal question that the court must decide.
10.5 Repayable Government Contributions as Assistance: CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2022 FCA 178)

In CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 57, aff'd CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178 (decided October 19, 2022), the Federal Court of Appeal addressed whether non-forgivable, unconditionally repayable loans provided by the federal Department of Industry under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) in the 2012 and 2013 taxation years constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act.

Applying the authoritative appellate principles established in Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co., [1987] 2 F.C. 60, Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc., [1996] F.C.J. No. 1226 (QL), and Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196, the Federal Court of Appeal (per Boivin J.A., De Montigny J.A., and Locke J.A.) upheld the Tax Court's ruling that because the terms of the government loan were not strictly commercial, the unconditionally repayable contributions constituted "government assistance" within the meaning of subsection 127(9), thereby both reducing CAE Inc.'s SR&ED ITCs and requiring inclusion in taxable income.
